targets.question: Let my AI run my Make scenarios as tools, and optionally build or edit them

pick.name: Make MCP Server (cloud)

access.scope_note: Two tool families. Scenario tools: every scenario that is active with on-demand scheduling becomes a callable tool, and it runs with whatever app connections the scenario holds. Management tools (paid plans only): view and modify scenarios and their connections, webhooks and data stores, plus teams and organisations, gated by scopes scenarios:read, scenarios:write, teams:write, organizations:write. OAuth at https://mcp.make.com lets you pick organisation and scopes on the consent screen. MCP-token mode (https://<zone>/mcp/u/<token>/stateless, or Bearer header) can be narrowed to one organisation, team or scenario with URL parameters. Docs list no delete tool; we could not confirm the write scopes cannot delete via management tools, so treat scenarios:write as destructive.

pick.cost: Scenario-run tools on all plans including Free. Management (build/edit) tools need a paid plan. Each run spends Make operations as normal.
pick.the_catch: The token flavour is the blast radius. An MCP token with mcp:use exposes every active on-demand scenario across all your Make organisations by default, and each scenario runs with its own stored app credentials, so the model inherits every Gmail, Sheets or database connection any of those scenarios uses. Narrow it with ?organizationId, ?teamId or ?scenarioId[] on the URL, and note those filters do nothing for management tools. The token also rides in the URL path, which lands in client logs and config files. Prefer OAuth. Separately: the OAuth endpoint times out scenario tools at 25 seconds and management tools at 30; the scenario keeps running for up to 40 minutes but the client gets nothing back unless you also granted scenarios:read so it can fetch the result later. The old local integromat/make-mcp-server on GitHub is labelled legacy; do not start there.

alternate.name: Make MCP Server (legacy local)

access.scope_note: Runs on-demand scenarios only, in one team, using a Make API key with scenarios:read and scenarios:run. No management tools. Effectively a narrower, run-only surface.

alternate.cost: Free; spends Make operations per run.
alternate.the_catch: README points you to the cloud version for most use cases. Useful only if you want a hard team-scoped, run-only key and no remote endpoint. Expect no new features.

targets.question: Give my AI a persistent memory it can write to and search across sessions

pick.name: Knowledge Graph Memory Server (@modelcontextprotocol/server-memory)

access.scope_note: Nine tools over a local JSONL file: create_entities, create_relations, add_observations, delete_entities, delete_observations, delete_relations, read_graph, search_nodes, open_nodes. Touches nothing but that one file, set with MEMORY_FILE_PATH. No way to switch the delete tools off short of your client's tool allow-list.

pick.cost: Free. MIT.
pick.the_catch: Set MEMORY_FILE_PATH or you will lose the memory. The default is memory.jsonl inside the package directory, and with npx -y that directory is replaced when the package updates, so the 'persistent' memory quietly resets. It is a single flat file with no locking: two clients pointed at it will clobber each other. read_graph returns the whole graph, so once the file grows the model pays for all of it on every recall; there is no pruning or ranking. And the repo says it plainly: reference implementation, educational, not production. Fine for one person on one machine, not for a shared agent.

targets.question: Give my AI a scratchpad tool for step-by-step reasoning with revisions and branches

pick.name: Sequential Thinking Server (@modelcontextprotocol/server-sequential-thinking)

access.scope_note: One tool, sequential_thinking. It takes the model's own thought text plus counters and revision/branch flags, logs it to stderr, and echoes structure back. No file, network or system access. DISABLE_THOUGHT_LOGGING=true silences the console output.

pick.cost: Free. MIT.
pick.the_catch: It does not think. It is a formatting loop: the model writes a thought, the tool hands it back, the model writes the next one. Every step is a tool round-trip, so a 15-thought chain is 15 extra calls and the whole chain sits in context. On models with built-in extended thinking it mostly duplicates what the model already does, at a token cost, and can make the model over-deliberate on trivial asks because the tool description tells it to. Leave thought logging on by default and your client's stderr fills with the model's private reasoning, which some hosts surface to users. Zero security surface, which is the one thing genuinely in its favour.

targets.question: Let my AI know the current time and convert between timezones reliably

pick.name: Time Server (mcp-server-time)

access.scope_note: Two tools: get_current_time(timezone) and convert_time(source_timezone, time, target_timezone), IANA names only. Reads the system clock and timezone database. Writes nothing. Override the detected local zone with --local-timezone=Europe/London.

pick.cost: Free. MIT.
pick.the_catch: It is Python, so unlike the other reference servers you need uv or pip on the machine, and 'uvx mcp-server-time' builds a fresh environment on first launch, so the first start is slow and fails outright if uv is not on the PATH the client uses. Timezone autodetection follows the container or server it runs in, not the user, so in Docker or on a remote box it happily reports UTC as 'local'; pass --local-timezone explicitly. If your client already injects the date and time into the system prompt (most do now), this server adds nothing but convert_time. Check that before installing.

targets.question: Let my AI act in any of my Zapier-connected apps (Gmail, Sheets, Slack, HubSpot...) through one connection

pick.name: Zapier MCP

access.scope_note: Endpoint https://mcp.zapier.com/api/v1/connect (Streamable HTTP only; no SSE). It reaches whatever Zapier connections you own, across 9,000+ apps and 40,000+ actions. Default mode is dynamic discovery: the agent gets discover_zapier_actions, enable_zapier_action, execute_zapier_read_action and execute_zapier_write_action, so it can find and switch on an action in any app you have connected mid-conversation. Alternative is manual configuration at mcp.zapier.com: you hand-pick each app, action and connection, and per field choose 'AI guesses', 'AI picks from these choices', 'fixed value' or 'default'. That is the only real narrowing. Deletes depend on the app; Zapier does not block destructive actions.

pick.cost: No separate MCP plan. Each successful tool call burns two tasks from your Zapier plan; 'email 3 people' is 3 calls, 6 tasks. Free-plan task quota runs out fast; failed calls are not charged.
pick.the_catch: Blast radius. One OAuth grant does not give the model one app, it gives it every app connection you personally own in Zapier, and in the default dynamic mode the model can enable new actions in any of them without you touching the dashboard. A prompt-injected agent asked to 'tidy up' can create, update or delete in your CRM, mail and drive with the same connection you set up for reading a spreadsheet. If you want a fence, use manual configuration, add only the actions you need, and pin fields to fixed values; there is no per-connection deny list. Then watch the meter: two tasks per call, and batch-style prompts multiply calls, so a chatty agent on a Starter plan hits the monthly cap and every tool silently starts returning errors until the reset. Connection-token auth exists for clients that cannot OAuth; that token is a bearer secret with the same reach.

targets.question: Let my AI trigger, inspect, and build workflows on my n8n instance

pick.name: n8n instance-level MCP server

access.scope_note: Built into n8n (cloud and self-hosted); switch on under Settings > Instance-level MCP, then flag each workflow 'Available in MCP'. Tools cover search/get/execute/test workflows, publish and unpublish, create_workflow_from_code and update_workflow (2.13+), archive_workflow, executions, projects, folders, tags, list_credentials (metadata only, never secrets), data tables (create, rename, add or delete columns, insert rows; no row reads or table deletes), and agent management (2.34+, preview). No delete_workflow tool; archive only. Scoped to the connecting user's permissions. OAuth (recommended, callback domains can be restricted) or a personal API key as Bearer.

pick.cost: Built into n8n; no extra charge stated. Self-hosted or Cloud, executions it triggers count as normal.
pick.the_catch: The per-workflow toggle looks like a fence but the build tools are the blast radius. Once a workflow is MCP-enabled the model can execute it with the workflow's stored credentials, and update_workflow has a setNodeCredential operation, so it can wire any credential you can see (list_credentials shows them all) into a node, publish, and run it. An 'Available in MCP' Slack notifier can become a 'read my Postgres and post it' workflow without a human opening the editor. Keep the connecting user least-privilege, or better, a dedicated project member with only the credentials the agent should touch. Also: access is not client-scoped. Every connected client sees every enabled workflow for that user; the only revoke is to disable MCP for the whole instance, which kicks all clients. Self-hosted behind a proxy? It must pass MCP-Protocol-Version, Mcp-Method and Mcp-Name headers or nothing works. Feature set is pinned to version: editing needs 2.13, agents 2.34, version diffs 2.36. Upgrade before you blame the client.

alternate.name: MCP Server Trigger node

access.scope_note: You build a workflow with the MCP Server Trigger and attach only the tool nodes you want exposed. Clients get exactly those tools, nothing else on the instance. Auth is none, Bearer token or custom header, chosen per trigger. SSE or Streamable HTTP; no stdio.

clients: any SSE or Streamable HTTP MCP client
alternate.cost: Free; each tool call is an execution on Cloud plans.
alternate.the_catch: Right answer when you want a tight, hand-built tool surface rather than instance access. But 'No auth' is a menu option and the path is a random string, which people treat as a secret. It is not. Queue-mode deployments must route all /mcp* traffic to one webhook replica or connections drop, and nginx needs proxy buffering off. The workflow has to be published for the production URL to answer.

targets.avoid: leonardsellem/n8n-mcp-server (and the npm package n8n-mcp-server). Widely linked, 1.6k stars, but the npm build is stuck at 0.1.0 from March 2025, it needs a full n8n API key, and it ships workflow_delete. n8n's built-in server replaced it.

targets.question: Let my AI read my CRM, create and update contacts, companies and deals, and log activity in HubSpot

pick.name: HubSpot Remote MCP Server (mcp.hubspot.com)
pick.auth: OAuth (2.1 with PKCE; via HubSpot's Claude/ChatGPT/Gemini/Copilot connectors or your own MCP Auth App)

access.scope_note: 25 tools. Reads CRM objects, activities, conversations, campaigns, content and marketing email analytics, including a SQL-style query_crm_data. Writes: manage_crm_objects creates or updates contacts, companies, deals, tickets, custom objects, line items, products and activities (calls, meetings, notes, tasks, emails); quotes are create/update in beta; marketing emails, landing pages, blog posts and campaigns can be created and published. No delete tools at all. Money: NONE. Invoices, orders, carts, payments and payment links are read-only; it cannot create a charge, refund a payment, or trigger a payout. Quotes can be drafted but not sent. Narrowing: you cannot pick scopes; they are derived from the tool set and capped by the connecting user's HubSpot permissions. Test mode: not documented. There is no sandbox switch in the MCP docs.

clients: Cursor / Claude Code / others via a self-made MCP Auth App
pick.cost: Free on any HubSpot tier for the HubSpot side; the Claude connector needs a paid Claude plan (Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise).
pick.the_catch: A Super Admin has to bless the first connection, and after that every user who connects gets write access equal to their own HubSpot permissions with no way to make the agent read-only. If you are not on Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini or Copilot you must create an MCP Auth App (public beta since January 2026) and your client has to do OAuth 2.1 with PKCE itself; HubSpot documents no client-specific setup for Cursor, VS Code or Windsurf. Bulk writes are capped at 10 records per call, and everything counts against your normal API limits.

alternate.name: @hubspot/mcp-server (local stdio, beta)

access.scope_note: 21 tools: list/search/batch-read objects, batch create and update, properties, associations, notes and tasks, workflows (read), link generation. No deletes. No commerce writes: nothing for invoices, payments, refunds or payouts. Narrowing is real here: the private app's scopes are exactly what you tick, so read-only is one checkbox away. Test mode: not documented.

alternate.cost: Free; private apps are on every tier.
alternate.the_catch: Still labelled beta and last published in June 2025; the GitHub repo HubSpot/mcp-server now shows empty. It is the only official route to a scope-limited, read-only HubSpot agent, but expect it to be quietly superseded by the remote server.

targets.question: Let my AI create and send PayPal invoices, look up transactions and disputes, and process refunds

pick.name: PayPal MCP Server (hosted, mcp.paypal.com / mcp.sandbox.paypal.com)
pick.auth: OAuth (remote) or API key (client-credentials access token, local)

access.scope_note: Tools: invoices (create, send, remind, cancel, QR code), payments (create_order, pay_order, get_order, create_refund, get_refund), disputes (list, get, accept_dispute_claim), shipment tracking, catalog products, subscription plans and subscriptions (create, update, cancel), list_transactions and get_merchant_insights; the remote server adds search_product, create_cart and checkout_cart. Money: charges YES in the sense that create_order plus pay_order captures an approved order, and send_invoice bills a customer; refunds YES (create_refund on a captured payment); payouts NO, there is no Payouts API tool. accept_dispute_claim concedes a chargeback, which is money out. No delete tools; cancel_subscription and cancel_sent_invoice are the closest. Narrowing: the local server's --tools flag selects tools; the remote server's OAuth grant is all-or-nothing. Test mode: yes, first-class. Remote has a separate sandbox host and the local server defaults to PAYPAL_ENVIRONMENT=SANDBOX.

clients: any MCP client (SSE at /sse or streamable HTTP at /http)
pick.cost: Free. Sandbox needs a Developer account; production needs a Business account.
pick.the_catch: accept_dispute_claim and create_refund both move money out with no confirmation built in, and on the remote server you cannot switch them off. Local tokens are client-credentials bearer tokens that expire after 3 to 8 hours, so the stdio setup silently dies mid-day and you re-paste. The npm package has not shipped since October 2025 and the docs' tool list already differs from the package README, so trust what the server advertises, not the docs.

targets.question: Let my AI query and update records in my Salesforce org from Claude, Cursor or ChatGPT

pick.name: Salesforce Hosted MCP Servers (SObject Reads / Mutations / Deletes / All)
pick.auth: OAuth (2.0 with PKCE via an External Client App with mcp_api and refresh_token scopes)

access.scope_note: Pick the server that matches the blast radius you want: sobject-reads (schema, SOQL, search, related records only), sobject-mutations (adds create/update, no delete), sobject-deletes, or sobject-all (everything: createSobjectRecord, updateSobjectRecord, deleteSobjectRecord and relatives). All respect the connecting user's object and field-level security. Custom servers can expose your own Flows, Apex actions and Named Queries. Money: NONE. Salesforce is not a payment processor; it can create Opportunity, Order or custom billing records but cannot charge a card, refund, or pay anyone out. Test mode: yes. Every server has a /sandbox/ path (https://api.salesforce.com/platform/mcp/v1/sandbox/platform/sobject-all) that serves sandboxes and scratch orgs.

pick.cost: Included with Enterprise Edition and above; no separate credits mentioned. Needs a System Administrator to enable servers and create the External Client App.
pick.the_catch: Setup is where people stall. Servers are off by default (Setup > API Catalog > MCP Servers, up to two minutes to activate) and you must build an External Client App with PKCE, JWT tokens and an exact callback URL per client (claude.ai/api/mcp/auth_callback for Desktop, localhost:38000/callback for Claude Code); a mismatch gives the 'Authorization with the MCP server failed' error that fills Anthropic's issue tracker. Deletes on sobject-all are real, though records sit in the Recycle Bin for 15 days. Enterprise Edition or higher only, so no Developer Edition tinkering on the hosted path.

alternate.name: Salesforce DX MCP Server (@salesforce/mcp)
alternate.auth: other (reuses Salesforce CLI org logins; --orgs flag picks which)

access.scope_note: Developer tooling, not CRM ops. Toolsets you opt into with --toolsets: data (run_soql_query only, no DML), metadata (deploy_metadata, retrieve_metadata), orgs (create/delete scratch orgs and snapshots), testing (Apex and agent tests), users (assign permission sets), devops, mobile, code analysis and LWC/Aura experts. No record create/update/delete tools. Money: none. Test mode: scratch orgs and sandboxes are the native unit; --orgs DEFAULT_TARGET_ORG keeps it off production unless you point it there.

alternate.cost: Free (Apache-2.0). Works on Developer Edition and scratch orgs.
alternate.the_catch: deploy_metadata will push to whatever org --orgs allows, and ALLOW_ALL_ORGS hands it every org your CLI has ever logged into, production included. It cannot insert or update records, so if you wanted a CRM agent this is the wrong server. Non-GA tools need --allow-non-ga-tools and change between weekly releases.

targets.question: Let my AI manage my Shopify store: orders, products, customers, inventory and refunds

pick.name: shopify-mcp (GeLi2001)
pick.auth: API key (Admin API access token shpat_… or client-credentials for a custom app)

access.scope_note: 31 tools over the Admin GraphQL API: products (create/update/delete, variants, options), customers (create/update/delete/merge, addresses), orders (get, update, cancel, close/open, mark-as-paid, create-fulfillment, refund-create, draft orders, complete-draft-order), metafields, inventory quantities and tags. Money: refunds YES (refund-create). Charges: no card charging; it can create and complete draft orders and mark orders paid, which records a sale but takes no payment. Payouts: no (Shopify Payments payouts are not exposed). Narrowing: only through the scopes you grant the custom app (read_/write_ products, customers, orders); there is no read-only flag in the server. Test mode: no explicit mode. Point it at a free Shopify development store with its own token; a development store's Bogus Gateway lets you test refunds without real money. Official picks exist but do not do this job: Shopify Dev MCP (docs and schema only, no store data) and Storefront MCP (public catalogue and cart, no auth, cannot see or change orders).

pick.cost: Free. Needs a custom app in your store admin; a development store is free via a Partner account.
pick.the_catch: This is one person's project with full write and delete over your live store, and it is the best on offer because Shopify has shipped no Admin MCP of its own as of September 2026. The delete-product, delete-customer and refund-create tools run with no confirmation step beyond what your client adds. If the custom-app token you paste has write_orders, the agent can refund. Last npm publish was February 2026; Shopify retires Admin API versions quarterly, so watch that the pinned 2026-01 version does not age out.

alternate.name: Shopify Dev MCP (@shopify/dev-mcp)

access.scope_note: Docs search, GraphQL schema introspection and code validation for Admin, Storefront, Functions, Polaris and Liquid. It never touches a store: no orders, no products, no refunds, no payouts, no test mode needed. Use it to write the Admin API calls your own agent will make, not to run them.

alternate.cost: Free.
alternate.the_catch: Builders keep installing it expecting store access and get a documentation bot. It also phones home with usage telemetry by default; set OPT_OUT_INSTRUMENTATION to stop that. Shopify's other official server, Storefront MCP at https://{shop}.myshopify.com/api/mcp, is public and unauthenticated by design: it can search the catalogue and build a cart, but checkout hands off to a URL, so it cannot charge, refund or read orders.

targets.avoid: Any hosted third-party 'Shopify MCP' proxy (there are dozens of forks named shopify-mcp-server on the registries) that asks you to paste a shpat_ Admin token into their service. That token is full write access to your store, none of them are vetted by Shopify, and most are thinner wrappers of the same Admin GraphQL calls you get from a local install.

targets.question: Let my AI work my Square account: customers, catalogue, orders, payments and refunds

pick.name: Square MCP Server (hosted, mcp.squareup.com; local square-mcp-server)

access.scope_note: Three meta-tools, get_service_info, get_type_info and make_api_request, expose the whole Square API surface (30+ services: payments, refunds, payouts, bank accounts, customers, orders, catalog, invoices, loyalty, subscriptions, team, and more). Money: charges YES, make_api_request can call Payments.create if it has a payment source id; refunds YES via the Refunds API; payouts READ ONLY, Square's Payouts API only lists and retrieves, so the agent can see settlements but cannot initiate them. Deletes are whatever the API allows (catalog objects, customers). Narrowing: locally, DISALLOW_WRITES=true makes it read-only; remotely you choose OAuth scopes at consent. Test mode: local only. SANDBOX=true with a sandbox token; the remote server 'only accesses production resources'.

pick.cost: Free; Beta. Needs a Square developer account (sandbox is free).
pick.the_catch: The hosted server is production-only, so the first place your agent can issue a refund or a customer delete is your real account. Square's own advice is to rehearse on a local sandbox instance first, which is a different auth path (raw access token in config). The generic make_api_request tool means the model composes arbitrary API calls; it will happily call any endpoint your token or OAuth grant allows. The local npm package has not moved since April 2025 and the whole thing is still labelled Beta.

targets.question: Let my AI look up customers and payments in Stripe, issue refunds, and create invoices or payment links

pick.name: Stripe MCP Server (hosted, mcp.stripe.com)
pick.auth: OAuth (or a restricted API key as a bearer token)

access.scope_note: Two generic tools, stripe_api_read and stripe_api_write, front an allow-list of ~150 API methods, plus dedicated create_refund, account, analytics, reporting and docs-search tools. Money: it CAN create refunds (create_refund), and can create Checkout Sessions, payment links, invoices, invoice items and subscriptions, which bill customers. It CANNOT create a charge or PaymentIntent directly (no create method is on the list; charges and PaymentIntents are list/retrieve only). It CANNOT create payouts, transfers or outbound payments; payouts, transfers, balance and Treasury/money-management objects are read-only. Only delete on the list is coupons. Narrowing: with OAuth you get whatever the consent screen grants per environment; with a restricted API key (rk_) you set exact per-resource read/write permissions yourself and can pass Stripe-Account for a Connect account. Test mode: yes. OAuth sessions and admin MCP access are managed separately for live mode and each sandbox, and rk_test_ keys work as bearer tokens.

clients: any MCP client with OAuth or a bearer header
pick.cost: Free. Needs a Stripe account; analytics and money-management tools are private/public preview.
pick.the_catch: The write tool is one blunt instrument: stripe_api_write covers every POST/PATCH/PUT/DELETE method on the allow-list, so a single OAuth consent gives the agent refunds, invoice finalisation, subscription cancellation, coupon deletion and dispute updates in whichever environment you authorised. Stripe itself tells you to turn on human confirmation of tool calls. If you connect in live mode by accident there is no dry run. Use a sandbox OAuth session or an rk_test_ key until you have watched the tool-call logs in Workbench.

alternate.name: @stripe/mcp (local stdio server)
alternate.auth: API key (secret or restricted key via --api-key)

access.scope_note: ~21 named tools (customers, products, prices, payment links, invoices, subscriptions, refunds, coupons, disputes, balance, docs search). Refunds: yes. Charges: no direct charge; payment links and invoices only. Payouts: no. The --tools flag lets you enable exactly the operations you want (e.g. --tools=customers.read,refunds.create), which the hosted server cannot do. Test mode: pass an sk_test_/rk_test_ key.

alternate.cost: Free.
alternate.the_catch: Stripe's docs no longer mention it; everything points at mcp.stripe.com and the CLI plugin. The key sits in plain text in your client config, and if you paste an sk_live_ key it has full account rights regardless of --tools. Version 0.3.3 in March 2026 is the last publish.

targets.avoid: The Stripe entries in third-party MCP registries that wrap the API with a single 'run any Stripe request' tool and ask for your sk_live_ key. Stripe's own hosted server already does that safely with OAuth and an allow-list; a wrapper of a wrapper adds nothing but a second place your secret key lives.

targets.question: Let my AI query and change resources in my AWS account

pick.name: AWS MCP Server (managed)

access.scope_note: Hosted at https://aws-mcp.us-east-1.api.aws/mcp (also eu-central-1). Tools: call_aws (any of 15,000+ API operations, including Delete*), search_documentation, read_documentation, run_script (Python, server-side sandbox, inherits your IAM permissions). Access is bounded by the IAM identity you sign in with. OAuth path needs the AWSMCPSignInOAuthAccessPolicy managed policy; SigV4 path goes through the open-source MCP Proxy for AWS, which adds a read-only mode and profile switching. Every call lands in CloudTrail.

pick.cost: No charge for the server. You pay for whatever it creates.
pick.the_catch: The easy OAuth setup has no read-only switch: the agent gets everything your IAM identity can do, and call_aws will terminate an instance or empty a bucket if the policy allows it. Read-only lives only on the SigV4 route via mcp-proxy-for-aws (needs AWS CLI 2.32+ and uv), or in a ReadOnlyAccess policy you write yourself. OAuth sessions are single-account, single-profile, and expire after 12 hours. Only two regional endpoints, though they call every region.

alternate.name: AWS API MCP Server (awslabs, local)

access.scope_note: Runs on your machine with your AWS profile. call_aws executes validated AWS CLI commands, suggest_aws_commands finds them. READ_OPERATIONS_ONLY_MODE=true blocks mutations; REQUIRE_MUTATION_CONSENT=true asks before each write (needs a client that supports elicitation). Local file access is limited to a working dir unless you open it up.

alternate.cost: Free (pip/uv package). You pay for what it creates.
alternate.the_catch: Not the same thing as the managed server, and easy to confuse. Runs with your local credentials and no sandbox; AWS says outright it is not for multi-tenant or shared use. Default is read-write; the read-only and consent flags are off until you set them.

targets.avoid: The awslabs Cloud Control API MCP server (awslabs.ccapi-mcp-server) is marked deprecated in the awslabs/mcp README; use the IaC server or the API server instead. Also note that awslabs dropped SSE transport in May 2025, so old remote configs for those local servers are dead.

targets.question: Let my AI manage Workers, DNS, KV, R2 and the rest of my Cloudflare account

pick.name: Cloudflare MCP Server (Code Mode)

access.scope_note: Hosted at https://mcp.cloudflare.com/mcp. Three tools: docs, search (JS against the OpenAPI spec) and execute (JS that calls cloudflare.request()). Whatever the token can do, execute can do, across ~2,500 endpoints: create and delete DNS records, Workers, KV namespaces, D1, R2, Access policies. Narrowing is entirely at the token: OAuth lets you pick permissions during authorisation, or bring a scoped API token as a bearer header. ?codemode=false swaps to one tool per endpoint.

pick.cost: Free to use. Some things it can create (Workers paid features, Browser Rendering, R2) bill your account.
pick.the_catch: execute runs model-written JavaScript against the full Cloudflare API with your token. There is no read-only switch and no destructive-tool gate; a DNS record or a Worker can be deleted in one call. Scope the token yourself, ideally an account token limited to the zones and products you need. API tokens with client IP filtering are refused. The repo has no tagged releases, so you cannot pin a version; you get whatever is deployed. Do not use the old *.mcp.cloudflare.com/sse URLs: legacy SSE now returns 410 Gone.

alternate.name: Cloudflare domain-specific MCP servers

access.scope_note: Sixteen narrower hosted servers at *.mcp.cloudflare.com/mcp with typed tools: Observability, Workers Bindings (KV, D1, R2, Hyperdrive), Workers Builds, Browser Rendering, Radar, Audit Logs, DNS Analytics, Logpush, AI Gateway, AutoRAG, CASB, DEX, GraphQL, docs. Most are read-only; Bindings and Builds write. Pick the one you need instead of the whole API.

alternate.cost: Free; some servers need a paid Workers plan.
alternate.the_catch: Better blast radius than Code Mode, worse coverage: no DNS records, no zone settings, no Access. The Observability server chains many tool calls and regularly blows the model's context window mid-answer.

sources.label: Cloudflare docs: MCP servers for Cloudflare

targets.question: Let my AI manage local containers, images and volumes

pick.name: Docker (CLI) server in the Docker MCP Catalog

access.scope_note: Defined in docker/mcp-registry as servers/docker: a single tool called docker that takes an args array and runs it in the docker:cli image with /var/run/docker.sock bind-mounted. Anything the docker CLI can do, including rm, rmi, system prune, run --privileged, and mounting host paths into new containers. No read-only mode and no tool-level narrowing; the Toolkit's allowlist is per tool, and there is only one tool.

pick.cost: Free. Needs Docker Desktop 4.43+ (4.62+ for the current MCP Toolkit UI).
pick.the_catch: It is a raw passthrough to the Docker socket, which is root on the host. The one tool accepts arbitrary CLI arguments, so the model can prune every image, kill your database container, or start a privileged container with / mounted, with nothing in between except your client's approval prompt. Docker's own MCP Toolkit sandboxing (1 CPU, 2 GB, no host filesystem) does not apply to what this tool tells the daemon to do. Install and reach it via the Docker MCP Toolkit / docker mcp gateway, not directly.

alternate.name: mcp-server-docker (ckreiling)

access.scope_note: Python server over the Docker SDK: list/create/run/start/stop/remove containers, pull/push/build/remove images, create/remove networks and volumes. Deliberately omits --privileged and cap-add/cap-drop. Talks to the local socket or DOCKER_HOST=ssh://.

alternate.cost: Free.
alternate.the_catch: Typed tools are safer than a CLI passthrough, but remove tools are on by default and there is no read-only flag. One maintainer, ~54 commits; the README itself warns not to hand it containers with secrets in env vars because the model sees them.

targets.avoid: docker/labs-ai-tools-for-devs is deprecated (README says so, last release June 2025) and points you to the Docker Desktop MCP Toolkit. Also: docker/hub-mcp is real and official but talks to Docker Hub repositories, not your local daemon, so it is the wrong answer to this question.

targets.question: Let my AI read and edit my repos, issues and pull requests

pick.name: GitHub MCP Server

access.scope_note: Default toolset is context, repos, issues, pull_requests, users. That includes create_or_update_file, push_files, merge_pull_request, delete_file and delete_repository. Narrow it with --toolsets / --tools / --read-only locally, or the /readonly and /x/{toolset} URL paths (or X-MCP-Readonly, X-MCP-Toolsets headers) on the remote server. Read-only mode overrides everything else. OAuth asks for scopes per call (repo, workflow, delete_repo, security_events...); a PAT only does what its scopes allow.

pick.cost: Free. Remote endpoint is hosted by GitHub; local needs Docker or the Go binary.
pick.the_catch: delete_repository ships in the default repos toolset. With OAuth the server will challenge for the delete_repo scope the first time the model tries it, so a careless 'approve' is one click from a deleted repo. Use the /readonly URL or --read-only until you trust the workflow. Remote server lives at api.githubcopilot.com; GitHub Enterprise Server users must run it locally. Each MCP host also needs its own GitHub/OAuth App registered for remote OAuth, so on lesser-known clients you end up on a PAT anyway.

targets.avoid: The old @modelcontextprotocol/server-github reference server. It now lives in modelcontextprotocol/servers-archived with the note that no security updates or bug fixes will be provided, and it still turns up in tutorials and registries.

targets.question: Let my AI work with my GitLab projects, MRs, pipelines and issues

pick.name: GitLab MCP Server

access.scope_note: Built into GitLab itself at https://<your-gitlab>/api/v4/mcp. Acts as the signed-in user with their permissions. Read tools cover issues, MRs, diffs, commits, pipelines, jobs, logs, files, wiki, search. Write tools: add_commit, add_branch, create_issue, save_merge_request, save_note, save_merge_request_review, accept_merge_request (merges), save_pipeline (run/retry/cancel), save_work_item, link_work_items. manage_pipeline can delete a pipeline. No read-only switch documented; narrowing is via the user's own role.

pick.cost: Free. Available on Free, Premium and Ultimate since GitLab 19.2 (was Premium-only before).
pick.the_catch: Still Beta. There is no read-only mode: accept_merge_request will merge and manage_pipeline will delete, gated only by your GitLab role. OAuth uses Dynamic Client Registration, rate-limited to 10 registrations per IP per hour, so a team behind one NAT will hit it during setup; admins can turn DCR off entirely and then you need a pre-registered OAuth app. Self-managed instances must be on 19.2+ for the Free tier and the admin must have the setting on.

alternate.name: GitLab MCP (zereight)

access.scope_note: Community server (npm @zereight/mcp-gitlab) over stdio, SSE or Streamable HTTP with a GitLab PAT or its own OAuth flow. GITLAB_PERMISSION_MODE=modify allows create/update but blocks every delete tool (including deletes via execute_graphql); read-only via the legacy GITLAB_READ_ONLY_MODE. GITLAB_TOOLSETS, GITLAB_TOOLS and GITLAB_DENIED_TOOLS_REGEX narrow further. Default mode includes delete tools.

alternate.cost: Free.
alternate.the_catch: Only worth it if your instance is older than 19.2 or your admin has the built-in server off. A PAT with api scope is full account access, and delete tools are exposed unless you set GITLAB_PERMISSION_MODE. There is an execute_graphql tool, which is a general-purpose escape hatch around whatever tool filtering you thought you had.

targets.avoid: The old @modelcontextprotocol/server-gitlab reference server. It now lives in modelcontextprotocol/servers-archived with the note that no security updates or bug fixes will be provided.

targets.question: Let my AI read and update Jira issues and Confluence pages

pick.name: Atlassian Rovo MCP Server

access.scope_note: Hosted at https://mcp.atlassian.com/v2/mcp. Cloud only. Covers Jira, JSM, Confluence, Bitbucket, Compass, Goals and Loom: search, read, create and update work items and pages as the signed-in user, with their existing permissions. No delete tools documented. Org admins can block OAuth client domains, switch API-token auth off, and apply IP allowlists; there is no server-side read-only mode.

pick.cost: Needs a paid Atlassian Cloud plan. Every call burns Rovo credits (roughly 1 to 10 per call), pooled per user per month; Standard gets 25 to 250, Premium 70 to 700. Overage is billed if enabled, otherwise calls stop until the first of the month.
pick.the_catch: It is metered. An agent that loops over a backlog will drain a team's monthly Rovo credit pool in an afternoon, and by default when credits are gone the tools silently stop until next month. Rovo also has to be enabled by an org admin before anyone can connect. Data Center / Server is not supported. The v1 endpoint (mcp.atlassian.com/v1/sse) is deprecated and will be force-switched to v2 tools on 1 March 2027.

alternate.name: mcp-atlassian (sooperset)

access.scope_note: Community Python server covering Jira and Confluence on both Cloud (API token, OAuth 2.0) and Server/Data Center (PAT; Jira 8.14+, Confluence 6.0+). 98 tools including jira_delete_issue and confluence_delete_page. READ_ONLY_MODE blocks writes; ENABLED_TOOLS allowlists specific tools. Runs via uvx, pip or Docker over stdio, SSE or Streamable HTTP.

alternate.cost: Free; no Rovo credits.
alternate.the_catch: The only credible route for Data Center or for dodging Rovo metering, but it runs on your machine with your token and jira_delete_issue / confluence_delete_page are on unless you set READ_ONLY_MODE or an ENABLED_TOOLS list. Verify the current release before relying on it.

targets.avoid: The Atlassian v1 endpoint (https://mcp.atlassian.com/v1/sse) still appears in most guides; it is deprecated and will be switched to v2 tools on 1 March 2027. Use /v2/mcp now.

sources.label: Get started with the Atlassian Rovo MCP Server

targets.question: Let my AI find, create and update Linear issues and projects

pick.name: Linear MCP Server

access.scope_note: Hosted at https://mcp.linear.app/mcp (Streamable HTTP; /sse is the deprecated fallback). Finds, creates and updates issues, projects, comments and similar as the signed-in user. Two ways to go read-only: request only the read scope at OAuth time, or connect to https://mcp.linear.app/mcp/readonly, which only ever exposes read tools. No delete tools documented. Bearer token / API key headers work for headless use.

pick.cost: Free with any Linear workspace. Enterprise-managed auth (Okta SAML) is an Enterprise feature.
pick.the_catch: The default endpoint grants write on the whole workspace you authorise; the /readonly URL is a separate connection you have to choose up front, not a toggle. One connection equals one workspace, so multi-workspace users configure it twice. Auth state lives in ~/.mcp-auth on the client and periodically needs clearing when the remote connection wedges. WSL users are pushed to the deprecated SSE endpoint.

targets.question: Let my AI read and edit files on my machine

pick.name: Filesystem MCP Server (reference)

access.scope_note: Only touches directories you allow, given as command-line args or supplied by the client through MCP Roots (roots replace the args entirely). Tools: read_text_file, read_media_file, read_multiple_files, list_directory, directory_tree, search_files, get_file_info, list_allowed_directories, plus write_file (overwrites), edit_file, create_directory and move_file (which deletes the source). No rm tool, but write_file can empty a file. No read-only flag in the npm build; run it in Docker with the mount marked ro for read-only.

pick.cost: Free.
pick.the_catch: The scope is whatever you type on the command line, and every tutorial types the home directory. That hands the model ~/.ssh, ~/.aws, browser profiles and your Keychain-adjacent files with write access. Give it one project directory. If your client supports Roots it silently replaces your args with its own root list, so a workspace-wide root in VS Code widens the scope without editing the config. There is no delete tool, but write_file overwrites without confirmation and move_file will happily rename a directory out from under you.

alternate.name: Filesystem server via Docker (mcp/filesystem)
alternate.maintainer: Model Context Protocol project; image built by Docker

access.scope_note: Same server, same tools, but each host directory is an explicit bind mount under /projects and any mount can be flagged ro. The container cannot see anything you did not mount.

alternate.cost: Free; needs Docker.
alternate.the_catch: Paths the model sees are /projects/..., not your real paths, so it will guess wrong and you will paste translations. Still the only way to get a genuinely read-only mount.

targets.question: Let my AI search errors, read stack traces and triage Sentry issues

pick.name: Sentry MCP

access.scope_note: Remote at https://mcp.sentry.dev/mcp with OAuth, or an explicit token via an Authorization: Sentry-Bearer header. Read: search_issues, search_events, get_issue_details, stack traces, traces, replays, profiles, releases, docs. Write: update_issue (resolve/assign), add_issue_note, create_project, create_team, create_dsn, update_dsn, update_project, add/remove_team_from_project, create/update/delete_uptime_monitor. Narrow with URL scoping (/{org} or /{org}/{project}) and ?skills=inspect,triage or ?disable-skills=seer. stdio mode needs a User Auth Token with org:read, project:read, project:write, team:read, team:write, event:write.

pick.cost: Free with a Sentry account. Seer-backed tools need Seer on your plan. Self-hosted stdio needs your own LLM API key for the natural-language search tools.
pick.the_catch: Unscoped, the default connection sees every org and project your account can, and the tools default to all skills, including write. Scope the URL to a project and pass ?skills=inspect,triage or the model will happily resolve issues and create projects. The search_issues and search_events tools are themselves LLM-powered: remote is fine, but the stdio/self-hosted build silently drops them unless you set EMBEDDED_AGENT_PROVIDER and a key. The npm package is at 0.39.0 while the GitHub Releases page lags at 0.36.0, so check npm for what you are actually running.

targets.avoid: The old @modelcontextprotocol/server-sentry reference server, now in modelcontextprotocol/servers-archived with no security updates or bug fixes.

targets.question: Let my AI inspect deployments and logs, and deploy to Vercel

pick.name: Vercel MCP

access.scope_note: Hosted at https://mcp.vercel.com. Same access as your Vercel user. Read: teams, projects, deployments, build logs, runtime logs and errors, Web Analytics, Agent Runs, toolbar threads, docs search. Write: deploy_to_vercel (preview or production, creates the project if missing), toolbar replies, and a purchase family (buy_domain, buy_credits, buy_addon, buy_pro) behind a quote-then-confirm flow. No env-var, domain-config or delete tools. No read-only mode or scope picker at OAuth time.

pick.cost: Free with any Vercel account. Purchase tools charge the team's card, non-refundable.
pick.the_catch: It can spend money. buy_domain, buy_credits, buy_addon and buy_pro execute real, non-refundable charges against the team payment method; the only guard is a five-minute idempotency key and whatever confirmation prompt your client shows for confirm: true. deploy_to_vercel with target: production ships straight to prod. Vercel also only accepts clients it has reviewed, so an unlisted MCP client simply cannot authorise. Claude.ai / Desktop needs Pro, Max, Team or Enterprise for custom connectors.

targets.question: Let my AI read and post in my Discord server through a bot, and help moderate it

pick.name: discord-mcp

access.scope_note: Runs as a bot token. Read, send, edit and delete messages; create, edit and delete channels; create, edit, delete and assign roles; kick, ban and timeout members; webhooks, scheduled events, invites, emoji, permission overwrites. Everything the bot's Discord permissions allow is exposed; the only narrowing is the permission set you give the bot in the Developer Portal.

clients: Any stdio or HTTP MCP client (README documents Docker HTTP and stdio; no per-client list)
pick.cost: Free. Needs a Discord bot with the right permissions and intents.
pick.the_catch: Discord has no first-party MCP server; this is a bot-token wrapper and it has every destructive tool (delete message, delete channel, ban, kick) with no confirmation of its own. Sending is instant and posts as the bot, so any send or moderation tool must stay behind your client's approval prompt, and give the bot the narrowest role you can. Two more traps: without the Message Content privileged intent, reads come back with empty text and nothing tells you why; and the bot can only manage roles below its own. It is Java and ships as a Docker image, not an npx one-liner.

alternate.name: discord-agent-mcp

access.scope_note: Bot-token Discord.js server with 71 tools across messaging, channels, threads, roles, moderation, events, auto-mod and slash commands. Includes delete and ban tools. Narrowing only via the bot's Discord permissions.

clients: Any stdio or HTTP MCP client (no per-client list in docs)
alternate.cost: Free. Needs a Discord bot.
alternate.the_catch: Widest surface, which is also the risk: 71 tools including bans and deletes, no built-in confirmation or read-only mode. Install is clone-and-build from source; no pinned release found. Last update seen 2026-08-29 via Glama.

targets.avoid: v-3/discordmcp. It tops most 'Discord MCP' directory lists but has two tools (send-message, read-messages) and two commits. Fine as a demo, not something to build on.

sources.label: Discord developer docs intro (no MCP server, only llms.txt)

targets.question: Let my AI search my inbox, read threads, and draft or send email

pick.name: Gmail MCP server (gmailmcp.googleapis.com)

access.scope_note: Eleven tools: search_threads, get_thread, get_message, list_drafts, list_labels (read); create_draft, create_label, label/unlabel thread and message (write). No send, reply, forward, trash or delete tools on the reference page. Scopes are gmail.readonly plus gmail.compose; you can request only gmail.readonly on your own OAuth client if you want a read-only connection.

clients: Any HTTP MCP client that does OAuth 2.0
pick.cost: Free, but needs a Google Cloud project, your own OAuth client, and enrolment in the Workspace Developer Preview Program.
pick.the_catch: It is Developer Preview: you apply to a Google programme, wait for a Google Group invite, create your own OAuth web client with the exact redirect URI for your MCP host, and you may not ship it in a public app before GA. Then note what it cannot do: there is no send tool. It drafts; a human presses send in Gmail. That answers the confirmation question by design, but if your use case is 'AI sends email', this server does not do it and you will end up bolting on the Gmail REST API. Endpoint: https://gmailmcp.googleapis.com/mcp/v1. Claude access requires a paid Claude plan.

targets.avoid: GongRzhe/Gmail-MCP-Server (@gongrzhe/server-gmail-autoauth-mcp). 1.2k stars, the most-recommended community Gmail server, and it can send, batch-delete and manage filters with no confirmation. The repo was archived on 3 March 2026 and is read-only. Do not build on it.

sources.label: Carly: Google's Gmail MCP is real but gated

targets.question: Let my AI check my availability and create, move or cancel events

pick.name: Google Calendar MCP server (calendarmcp.googleapis.com)

access.scope_note: Nine tools: list_calendars, list_events, search_events, get_event, suggest_time (read); create_event, update_event, respond_to_event, delete_event (write/delete). The configure page only lists read-only scopes (calendarlist.readonly, events.freebusy, events.readonly), so what your consent screen grants for the write tools is not documented. If you want read-only, request only those three on your own OAuth client.

clients: Any HTTP MCP client that does OAuth 2.0
pick.cost: Free, but needs a Google Cloud project, your own OAuth client, and enrolment in the Workspace Developer Preview Program.
pick.the_catch: delete_event and update_event are live tools with no server-side confirmation; the model can cancel a meeting with attendees and Google mails everyone. Gate write tools in your client. Same Developer Preview gating as Gmail: apply, wait, build your own OAuth client, and do not ship publicly before GA. The docs list only read-only scopes while shipping write tools, so check the consent screen rather than the page. Endpoint: https://calendarmcp.googleapis.com/mcp/v1.

alternate.name: google-calendar-mcp (@cocal/google-calendar-mcp)

access.scope_note: Stdio by default, HTTP via Docker. Tools: list-calendars, list-events, search-events, get-event, get-freebusy, create/update/delete event, respond-to-event, multi-account. Requests the full calendar and calendar.events scopes; not narrowable without editing the code.

alternate.cost: Free; needs your own Google Cloud OAuth client.
alternate.the_catch: Same delete-without-confirmation problem as Google's server, and it asks for full read/write on every calendar. OAuth tokens live on local disk, and while your Google Cloud app is in 'testing' the token expires every 7 days and you re-authenticate. Pick it if you cannot get into Google's preview programme.

targets.question: Let my AI send transactional email and manage my Resend account

pick.name: Resend MCP Server

access.scope_note: Full Resend API: send single and batch emails (HTML, attachments, cc/bcc, scheduling), list, cancel and update sends; broadcasts to audiences; contacts, segments, templates, automations, domains, webhooks, API keys, suppressions, logs and received mail. Remote uses OAuth browser login or a bearer API key; local stdio uses RESEND_API_KEY. Narrow it by using a Resend API key with sending-only permission rather than full access.

pick.cost: Free server; sends count against your Resend plan and need a verified domain.
pick.the_catch: send-email and send-broadcast fire immediately with no confirmation step in the server; one hallucinated recipient list on a broadcast goes to your whole audience. The README has no guidance on gating sends, so it is on you: approve every send tool in the client, and for automation use a sending-only API key on a test domain first. Note the local server nags for a sender address on every call unless you set SENDER_EMAIL_ADDRESS. Remote endpoint: https://mcp.resend.com/mcp, updated to the 2026-07-28 spec in August.

targets.avoid: Hawstein/resend-mcp and PSU3D0/resend-mcp. Both predate the official server, share its name, and still surface in directories. The official one is a superset.

sources.label: Resend changelog: remote MCP supports 2026-07-28 spec

targets.question: Let my AI search my Slack, read channels and threads, and post messages as me

pick.name: Slack MCP Server

access.scope_note: Acts as you, with your user token: search messages and files, read channel history, threads, canvases, lists and profiles; send messages, draft messages, create channels and group DMs, react, upload files, create and update canvases and lists. No delete tools. You cannot narrow scopes per connection; you get whatever the client app's fixed manifest asks for, filtered by what your account can already see.

pick.cost: Free to connect; you sign in with your existing Slack account. No plan restriction stated in the docs.
pick.the_catch: You cannot just point a client at https://mcp.slack.com/mcp. Only Marketplace-published or workspace-internal Slack apps with a fixed, hard-coded app ID may use it (no Dynamic Client Registration, no SSE), so a custom client means building and registering your own Slack app, and a workspace admin must approve it. On sending: the send tool posts straight to any conversation as you, no built-in confirmation. There is a separate draft tool that previews inside the client, but nothing forces the model to use it. Keep sends behind your client's tool-approval prompt. Message search and send also sit on their own tighter rate limits.

targets.avoid: Pre-2026 community 'Slack MCP' servers built on bot or xoxc/xoxd browser tokens (the pattern behind most 'slack-mcp-server' repos in directories). Browser-token scraping is against Slack's terms, and Slack's own docs say not to mix community servers with the official one. The official server now covers read and send; use it.

sources.label: Guide to Model Context Protocol in Slack (help centre)
Slack blog: MCP server and RTS API generally available, 17 Feb 2026

targets.question: Let my AI read my Telegram chats and send messages for me

pick.name: telegram-mcp

access.scope_note: Logs in as your personal account over MTProto (Telethon) with an API id/hash and a session string. 80-plus tools: read history and search, send, edit, delete, forward, pin, schedule, react; manage contacts, groups, admin rights, bans, profile and privacy settings. A session string is full account access; there is no scope system to narrow it. File-path tools are off unless you set allowed roots.

clients: Any stdio, HTTP or SSE MCP client (README shows Claude Desktop and Cursor config)
pick.cost: Free. Needs api_id and api_hash from my.telegram.org.
pick.the_catch: This is a userbot. It is your account, and Telegram throttles, flags and can ban accounts automated over the user API; the README tells you to read the API terms first. On sending: send_message goes out as you with no confirmation beyond a contact-alias check that only guards against sending to the wrong person, not against sending at all. Keep send, delete and admin tools behind your client's approval prompt. Do not pip install 'telegram-mcp': the project says it does not control that PyPI name. Install from the repo.

alternate.name: mcp-telegram

access.scope_note: MTProto user-account login, but read-only by design: list dialogs and fetch unread messages. Sending and mark-as-read are unimplemented. Still full account credentials on disk.

alternate.cost: Free. Needs api_id and api_hash.
alternate.the_catch: Read-only is the point, so it cannot send, which sidesteps the confirmation question entirely. Same account-ban exposure as any userbot, and a much smaller surface with slow updates. Pick it if all you want is 'summarise my unread'.

targets.avoid: Bot API wrappers such as guangxiangdebizi/telegram-mcp are safer for your account but cannot read chat history (Bot API limitation) and this one has 2 stars and no releases. Also avoid installing anything named telegram-mcp from PyPI: the name is not held by the main project.

sources.label: Carly: no official Telegram server, ban risk

targets.question: Let my AI send SMS, place calls and manage my Twilio account

pick.name: Twilio MCP (@twilio-alpha/mcp)

access.scope_note: Generated from Twilio's OpenAPI specs, so it exposes the whole public API: send messages, start calls, buy and release numbers, delete resources. Auth is AccountSid/ApiKey:ApiSecret. You narrow by passing --services and --tags to limit which API groups load, and by using a restricted Twilio API key.

clients: Any stdio MCP client (README: any MCP-compatible assistant; no per-client list)
pick.cost: Free server; every SMS or call it triggers is billed to your Twilio account.
pick.the_catch: It is alpha (0.0.3, March 2025, no release since) and by default it loads every Twilio API into context, which is too many tools for most clients and includes send-SMS and release-number with no confirmation of its own. Each send costs real money, so restrict with --services, use a Twilio API key scoped to one subaccount, and keep messaging tools behind your client's approval prompt. Twilio's own security advisory says not to run community Twilio MCP servers alongside it.

alternate.name: Twilio hosted MCP server (mcp.twilio.com/docs)

access.scope_note: Two tools, twilio__search and twilio__retrieve, that search and return Twilio API operation schemas. It does not call the Twilio API and cannot touch your account. No credentials at all.

alternate.cost: Free public beta, no account needed, rate-limited.
alternate.the_catch: It is documentation, not an integration. Point your coding agent at it and it writes better Twilio code; point a chat assistant at it expecting to send a text and nothing happens. Nothing to confirm because it cannot act.

targets.avoid: Third-party Twilio MCP wrappers on directory sites. Twilio's security advisory explicitly warns against running community servers next to its own, since they hold the same account credentials.

sources.label: Twilio blog: Introducing the Twilio MCP Server and Skills, 7 May 2026

targets.question: Let my AI explore datasets and run SQL in BigQuery

pick.name: BigQuery MCP server (Google-managed remote)

access.scope_note: Endpoint https://bigquery.googleapis.com/mcp, GA. Google OAuth 2.0 with scope bigquery; the caller needs roles/mcp.toolUser plus bigquery.jobUser and dataViewer. Tools: list_dataset_ids, list_table_ids, get_dataset_info, get_table_info, execute_sql, execute_sql_readonly. execute_sql runs DML, DDL and Python UDFs, so DROP TABLE and DELETE work if the identity can. execute_sql_readonly rejects mutations. Docs say the only non-read-only tool is execute_sql, and the supported way to block it is an IAM deny policy on read-write MCP tool use. Hard limits: 3-minute query timeout, 3,000 rows back, no Drive external tables.

pick.cost: No charge for the MCP server itself. Every execute_sql is a normal BigQuery job billed by bytes scanned. No MCP-specific quotas; BigQuery API quotas apply.
pick.the_catch: Both execute_sql and execute_sql_readonly are offered to the model at once. Nothing stops it picking the read-write one, and a DELETE with no WHERE is a valid BigQuery job. Read-only is not a switch you flip on the server; it is an IAM deny policy you have to write against the read-write tool attribute. Also the model has no idea what a query costs: an unpartitioned full scan on a big table is one tool call away, with no dry-run in the loop.

alternate.name: MCP Toolbox for Databases (--prebuilt bigquery)

access.scope_note: Local Go binary, toolbox --prebuilt bigquery, auth via Application Default Credentials (or BIGQUERY_USE_CLIENT_OAUTH). Adds forecast, analyze_contribution, ask_data_insights and search_catalog. The source's writeMode defaults to allowed; set writeMode: blocked to make execute_sql SELECT-only, and allowedDatasets to fence it to named datasets.

alternate.cost: Free, Apache-2.0, self-hosted. BigQuery jobs bill as usual.
alternate.the_catch: writeMode: blocked and allowedDatasets are not available through the one-line --prebuilt flag; you have to write your own tools.yaml to set them. The prebuilt config is read-write with whatever ADC identity is lying around on your laptop, which is often an Owner.

sources.label: Google Cloud MCP supported products (GA status)
Google Cloud blog, remote BigQuery MCP (Jan 2026)

targets.question: Let my AI query and manage MongoDB collections and Atlas clusters

pick.name: MongoDB MCP Server

access.scope_note: Local (npx mongodb-mcp-server, stdio or --transport http) authenticates with a connection string, or Atlas API service-account client id/secret for cluster tools. readOnly defaults to false, so find, insert-many, update-many, delete-many, drop-collection, drop-database and create/drop-index are all live. --readOnly limits to read, connect and metadata. --disabledTools takes tool names, operation types (create/update/delete) or categories (atlas/mongodb). drop-database, drop-collection, delete-many and two Atlas tools ask for confirmation by default, and since 2.1.0 so do aggregations with $out/$merge. There is also an Atlas-managed remote server at https://mcp.mongodb.com (OAuth, Atlas only, read-only enforced by default, revoke per client in Atlas). Telemetry is on unless you set DO_NOT_TRACK=1.

pick.cost: Free, Apache-2.0. Local runs anywhere; the managed server needs an Atlas project.
pick.the_catch: The confirmation prompt on drop-database is only as good as your client. The README says it plainly: if the client does not support elicitation, the tool runs without confirmation. So on a client without elicitation, the default config will drop a database when asked. Set --readOnly or --disabledTools delete for anything you care about. And 2.0 changed the tool contract (every DB call now needs an explicit connection id), so older prompts and tutorials fail.

alternate.name: MongoDB Atlas Managed MCP Server

access.scope_note: Hosted at https://mcp.mongodb.com. OAuth via Atlas App Connections for interactive clients, service-account client credentials for agents. Org admins must opt in. Read-only enforcement is on by default and set per configuration; access control is project-level rather than collection-level. Atlas clusters only; not self-managed MongoDB.

alternate.cost: Needs an Atlas project. No separate MCP charge documented.
alternate.the_catch: Coarser than the local server: you cannot scope it to a single collection, only a project. Clients without native OAuth need the npx mongodb-atlas-mcp-remote shim, which is on a 3.0 prerelease track as of late August 2026. Plan/tier requirements are not stated in the docs.

sources.label: MongoDB MCP docs overview (local vs Atlas managed)

targets.question: Let my AI create branches, run SQL and manage my Neon Postgres projects

pick.name: Neon MCP Server (remote)

access.scope_note: Endpoint https://mcp.neon.tech/mcp. Full-access default: run_sql and run_sql_transaction execute arbitrary SQL; delete_project, delete_branch and reset_from_parent are all tools; plus compute endpoints, Neon Auth, Data API, storage. Read-only exists three ways: untick 'Full access' in the OAuth consent screen, append ?readonly=true, or the legacy x-read-only header. In read-only mode run_sql stays but only for SELECT and schema inspection; write and management tools are removed. An API key inherits the key's org/project scope. If you use IP Allow, whitelist Neon's two static MCP IPs.

pick.cost: Free with a Neon account. SQL you run bills as normal compute.
pick.the_catch: delete_project is a tool, and the docs tell you to never point it at production. The local npm package @neondatabase/mcp-server-neon is deprecated (last 0.6.5, Sep 2025) and its old /sse endpoint goes 410 on 1 Oct 2026, so tutorials that use either will break. Also: the hosted server is updated continuously with no versioned releases, so a tool you relied on last week can change shape without a changelog line you were watching.

alternate.name: DBHub (pointed at the branch's connection string)

access.scope_note: Plain Postgres over a Neon branch connection string. No project or branch management at all, so no delete_project by accident. --readonly for BEGIN READ ONLY plus a keyword filter.

alternate.cost: Free, MIT, self-hosted.
alternate.the_catch: Loses the thing that makes Neon nice for agents: creating a throwaway branch to test a migration. You get SQL, nothing more.

targets.avoid: The stdio package @neondatabase/mcp-server-neon. Neon marked it deprecated on npm and the README says it is no longer maintained. Use the remote endpoint.

targets.question: Let my AI query (and maybe change) a Postgres database

pick.name: DBHub

access.scope_note: Default is read-write. execute_sql takes arbitrary SQL, multiple statements, BEGIN/COMMIT blocks. It will run DROP TABLE and DELETE if the DSN's user can. Add --readonly and it does two things: a keyword allow-list (SELECT, SHOW, DESCRIBE, EXPLAIN) and BEGIN READ ONLY at the Postgres level. Bytebase's own docs say a privileged role can still get round it via functions, so pair it with a read-only DB user. --max-rows caps SELECT output. Only two tools by default (execute_sql, search_objects); explain_sql and health_check are opt-in. Auth is whatever is in the DSN string.

pick.cost: Free, MIT. You host it (npx, Docker image bytebase/dbhub, or .mcpb bundle). Needs Node 22.5+.
pick.the_catch: Nothing is read-only until you say so. The quick-install paths (Claude Code plugin, MCP bundle) prompt for a DSN and off you go, in read-write. And --readonly is a keyword filter plus a read-only transaction, not a sandbox: a superuser DSN can still call file or extension functions. Give it a role with SELECT only and treat --readonly as a second seatbelt, not the first.

alternate.name: Postgres MCP Pro

access.scope_note: Two modes. Unrestricted is the default and runs any SQL, including DROP and DELETE. --access-mode=restricted wraps queries in read-only transactions, parses out COMMIT/ROLLBACK escape attempts, and adds a statement timeout. README warns that unsafe procedural languages on the server can still bypass it. Extra tools: index tuning, EXPLAIN analysis, health checks. Auth is the DATABASE_URI connection string. stdio or SSE.

alternate.cost: Free, MIT. Self-hosted via pipx/uv or Docker.
alternate.the_catch: Last release was v0.3.0 in May 2025. Thirty-odd PRs sit open, including one (July 2026) that would flip the default to restricted and another (Aug 2026) blocking dangerous functions in FROM clauses. Neither is merged. So today: default is unrestricted, and restricted mode has known gaps. Good analysis tools, but you are running 16-month-old code against your database.

targets.avoid: @modelcontextprotocol/server-postgres, Anthropic's old reference server. Still the top hit in many tutorials. It was archived in May 2025, the npm package is marked unsupported, and Datadog Security Labs (Aug 2025) showed its 'read-only' transaction could be escaped with an injected COMMIT followed by arbitrary SQL. No fix is coming.

sources.label: Datadog: SQL injection in the Postgres MCP server

targets.question: Let my AI read and write keys, streams, JSON and vector indexes in Redis

pick.name: Redis MCP Server

access.scope_note: stdio only; README says streamable-http is 'future'. Auth is a redis:// or rediss:// URL, username/password flags, or Azure Entra ID. Tools cover strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, streams (including delete), JSON, pub/sub, vector search, plus a misc set with delete, expire and rename. There is no read-only flag and no tool filter in the server. The only way to narrow it is a Redis ACL user: e.g. -@dangerous -@write +@read. No FLUSHALL tool, but delete on a scanned key list gets you most of the way.

pick.cost: Free, MIT. Self-hosted via uvx or Docker image mcp/redis.
pick.the_catch: No read-only mode exists in the server, full stop. Every example config uses redis://localhost:6379/0 with the default user, which has ACL 'allcommands allkeys'. If you connect it to a real instance that way, the model can delete or rename any key and expire whatever it likes. Create an ACL user first. Also stdio-only, so no shared remote deployment without a proxy.

alternate.name: MCP Toolbox for Databases (Redis source)

access.scope_note: You write a tools.yaml; each tool is a command you define. Nothing is exposed that you did not author, so read-only is a matter of only writing read tools. Redis and Valkey sources supported.

alternate.cost: Free, Apache-2.0, self-hosted Go binary or container.
alternate.the_catch: More work: no prebuilt Redis tool set, so you author every tool. Good for a locked-down production surface, tedious for exploration.

targets.question: Let my AI query a local SQLite file

pick.name: DBHub

access.scope_note: DSN sqlite:///path/to/file.db, using Node's built-in node:sqlite so no native build. Default is read-write: execute_sql runs any statement, including DROP and DELETE, and multi-statement batches. --readonly does a keyword allow-list plus PRAGMA query_only = ON on the connection, which SQLite itself enforces. --max-rows caps result size. Two tools by default. No auth because there is none in SQLite; file permissions are your access control.

pick.cost: Free, MIT. Needs Node 22.5+ (for node:sqlite).
pick.the_catch: The path in the DSN is the whole security model. Point it at the app's live .db and the default mode will happily VACUUM, DROP and DELETE it while the app is running. Copy the file or add --readonly. And check your Node version first: older Node has no node:sqlite and the error is unhelpful.

alternate.name: mcp-sqlite

access.scope_note: stdio via npx mcp-sqlite. Tools: db_info, list_tables, get_table_schema, create_record, read_records, update_records, delete_records, and a query tool for arbitrary SQL. No read-only flag.

alternate.cost: Free, MIT.
alternate.the_catch: No read-only mode at all. The query tool runs anything. One-maintainer project; last release April 2026.

targets.avoid: The reference sqlite server from modelcontextprotocol/servers (Python mcp-server-sqlite, last PyPI 2025-04-25). It was moved to servers-archived in May 2025, where the README says the servers are no longer maintained and carry no security guarantees.

targets.question: Let my AI query Snowflake, with Cortex Analyst and Search where they exist

pick.name: Snowflake-managed MCP server

access.scope_note: You create it in SQL: CREATE MCP SERVER ... FROM SPECIFICATION with a YAML tool list, served at https://<account>/api/v2/databases/<db>/schemas/<schema>/mcp-servers/<name>. GA. Tool types: SYSTEM_EXECUTE_SQL, CORTEX_ANALYST_MESSAGE, CORTEX_SEARCH_SERVICE_QUERY, CORTEX_AGENT_RUN, and GENERIC for your own UDFs and procedures. Only tools you list exist. SYSTEM_EXECUTE_SQL takes config read_only: true, query_timeout and warehouse; the docs example sets read_only true but the CREATE MCP SERVER reference example omits config entirely, and nothing says the default is read-only, so assume writes are allowed unless you set it. Everything runs under the session's role (OAuth sessions use the user's DEFAULT_ROLE), so RBAC is the real limit. OAuth via a security integration; PATs work but Snowflake discourages them. Max 50 tools per server, 250 KB response cap.

pick.cost: No separate MCP charge documented. Every SQL tool call runs on the named warehouse and burns credits; Cortex tools bill as Cortex.
pick.the_catch: read_only is per tool and opt-in. Leave it off and SYSTEM_EXECUTE_SQL runs DROP or DELETE under whatever DEFAULT_ROLE the user carries, which for the person setting this up is often ACCOUNTADMIN. Snowflake advertises other roles in the OAuth flow but the session still uses DEFAULT_ROLE, so switching to a narrow role means changing the user's default, not just consenting differently. Not available in government regions.

alternate.name: MCP Toolbox for Databases (Snowflake source)

access.scope_note: Local server; you author tools.yaml with snowflake-sql (parameterised, you write the SQL) and snowflake-execute-sql (arbitrary SQL from the model). Read-only is whatever you choose to expose. Auth is username/password only; role defaults to ACCOUNTADMIN, warehouse to COMPUTE_WH.

alternate.cost: Free, Apache-2.0, self-hosted. Warehouse credits as usual.
alternate.the_catch: The Snowflake source defaults role to ACCOUNTADMIN and only supports password auth: no key pair, no OAuth, no PAT. Set role explicitly and skip snowflake-execute-sql if you want it read-only.

targets.avoid: Snowflake-Labs/mcp, the open-source server most blog posts link. Its README now says it is deprecated and no longer maintained, and its sample config sets Delete, Drop and TruncateTable permissions to true. Use the managed server.

sources.label: Snowflake release note 2026-08-07 (MCP GA in Native Apps)

targets.question: Let my AI work on my Supabase projects: schema, SQL, edge functions, logs

pick.name: Supabase MCP Server

access.scope_note: Hosted at https://mcp.supabase.com/mcp. Default enables every feature group except Storage: database (execute_sql, apply_migration), debugging, development, edge functions (deploy_edge_function), account (create_project, pause_project, confirm_cost), docs, branching (delete_branch, reset_branch; paid plans). execute_sql runs whatever SQL it is given, DDL and DELETE included. Narrow with query params: ?read_only=true runs all SQL as a read-only Postgres user and drops mutating tools; ?project_ref=xxx pins it to one project and hides account tools; ?features=database,docs picks groups. OAuth 2.1 by default; a PAT for CI. Local dev: the Supabase CLI serves it at localhost:54321/mcp with a smaller tool set and no OAuth.

pick.cost: Free with any Supabase account. Branching tools need a paid plan. create_project and confirm_cost can spend money on your org.
pick.the_catch: Out of the box it is a developer-scoped, read-write, all-projects connection. It can pause a project, deploy an edge function, and run DROP TABLE, all in one session. Supabase's own guidance is blunt: use a development project, never production, and keep manual tool approval on because prompt injection via data in your tables is a real vector. The safe URL is not the default one; you have to type ?project_ref=...&read_only=true yourself.

alternate.name: DBHub (pointed at the project's Postgres)

access.scope_note: Use the project's Postgres connection string (ideally a dedicated role) as the DSN. You get SQL only: no edge functions, logs, branching or account tools, which is the point. --readonly adds a keyword allow-list plus BEGIN READ ONLY.

alternate.cost: Free, MIT, self-hosted.
alternate.the_catch: You hand it a Postgres password in a config file. Make that a purpose-built role, not the postgres superuser Supabase shows you in the dashboard, or --readonly is decorative.

targets.question: Let my AI create, edit and export designs in my Canva account

pick.name: Canva MCP Server

access.scope_note: Endpoint https://mcp.canva.com/mcp. Reads: search-designs, get-design, get-design-pages, get-design-content, get-presenter-notes, get-assets, list-folder-items, search-folders, get-design-thumbnail. Writes: generate-design, create-design-from-candidate, import-design-from-url, copy-design, the editing transaction trio (start/perform/commit), upload-asset-from-url, create-folder, move-item-to-folder, comment-on-design, reply-to-comment, export-design. Plan-gated: resize-design and search-brand-templates (Pro+), autofill-design (Enterprise). No delete tool exists. Scope is the signed-in user's whole Canva account; there is no per-folder or read-only grant. Every user does their own OAuth.

pick.cost: Free to connect. What you can do follows your Canva plan: resize needs Pro+, autofill and brand templates need Enterprise, some export formats and premium elements need licences.
pick.the_catch: It writes to your real workspace, and commit-editing-transaction is final. There is no delete tool, which sounds safe until you realise there is no undo either: a bad edit is a bad edit in the design your team is presenting tomorrow. Rate limits are per tool and low on the expensive ones: 20/min for generate, edit-commit, export and copy. Auth needs a client that speaks CIMD (or the deprecated DCR); anything else means manual client registration. Do not confuse this with Canva's 'Dev MCP server' (npx @canva/cli mcp), which only serves Canva documentation to help you build Canva apps and cannot touch designs.

targets.avoid: Community packages such as mattcoatsworth/canva-mcp-server predate the official server and wrap the Connect API with your own OAuth app. Canva's own hosted server covers the same ground with no app registration; there is no reason to run a third-party one against your account.
